note: Recommended pedagogical dependencies, not universal scientific necessities. All required edges use AND semantics. Framework alternatives and optional branches are explicit. Estimates are rough hands-on study hours, not completion promises.

nodes.title: Python essentials
nodes.summary: Values, control flow, functions, collections and files let you turn an idea into a repeatable program. Separate input, transformation and output; add a small test before growing the script.
nodes.question: Why use a dictionary instead of a list for lookup by document ID?
nodes.answer: A dictionary maps unique keys to values and offers average constant-time key lookup. A list is ordered and usually needs a scan to find a matching ID. Neither removes the need to handle missing data.
nodes.project: Write a function that counts words in three strings; test empty input and repeated words.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Write a function that counts words in three strings; test empty input and repeated words.

nodes.title: Git & reproducible work
nodes.summary: A repository records changes; a commit captures a coherent version. Keep source and small fixtures in Git, secrets and generated model weights outside it. Save the command that reproduces your result.
nodes.question: How does a commit differ from a backup of your entire laptop?
nodes.answer: A commit records tracked project files and their history. It does not automatically include ignored files, untracked files, environments or external datasets. Back those up separately.
nodes.project: Create a local repository, commit a tiny script and its test, then inspect a diff.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Create a local repository, commit a tiny script and its test, then inspect a diff.

nodes.title: Terminal & Linux basics
nodes.summary: Learn paths, working directories, processes and environment variables. PowerShell is sufficient for the supplied Windows launcher; Linux skills help when you move a static library to a Pi.
nodes.question: Why can a relative path work in one terminal and fail in another?
nodes.answer: A relative path is resolved from the current working directory. Use an explicit project directory or derive paths from the script location.
nodes.project: List a project directory, run a script from its root and explain the resulting file paths.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: List a project directory, run a script from its root and explain the resulting file paths.

nodes.title: Probability
nodes.summary: Probabilities describe uncertainty. Conditional probability changes the sample space; independent events are a special case. Simulations approximate expectations and should include a seed when reproducibility matters.
nodes.question: Is P(A given B) generally equal to P(B given A)?
nodes.answer: No. Bayes rule connects them through P(A) and P(B). Rare-event base rates can change the conclusion even when a test has high sensitivity.
nodes.project: Simulate a biased coin and compare empirical frequency with its specified probability.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Simulate a biased coin and compare empirical frequency with its specified probability.

nodes.title: Statistics & measurement
nodes.summary: Separate an estimate from uncertainty about that estimate. Training, validation and final test sets serve different purposes. Repeatedly tuning against the final test set leaks information into your choices.
nodes.question: Why does a high training score not establish generalization?
nodes.answer: The model or your choices may fit training-specific patterns. Evaluate once on held-out examples and examine sample size, uncertainty and distribution shift.
nodes.project: Split a small dataset before fitting a baseline; report both training and held-out errors.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Split a small dataset before fitting a baseline; report both training and held-out errors.

nodes.title: Linear algebra
nodes.summary: Vectors represent collections of numbers; matrices describe linear maps. Track shapes before implementing a model. A dot product is a scalar, while an outer product is a matrix.
nodes.question: What is the shape of A @ B when A is 3 by 4 and B is 4 by 2?
nodes.answer: The result is 3 by 2. The shared inner dimension must match; reversing the multiplication is not generally valid.
nodes.project: Implement a dot product and matrix multiplication for small lists; test shape mismatches.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Implement a dot product and matrix multiplication for small lists; test shape mismatches.

nodes.title: Calculus & gradients
nodes.summary: A derivative measures local sensitivity. The chain rule connects derivatives through a computation. A gradient gives sensitivities with respect to multiple parameters; gradient descent moves against it.
nodes.question: Why compare an analytic gradient with a finite-difference estimate?
nodes.answer: They are independent ways to approximate the same local derivative. Agreement at sensible step sizes helps detect implementation errors; floating-point error limits very small steps.
nodes.project: Check the derivative of a quadratic numerically and show one gradient-descent step.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Check the derivative of a quadratic numerically and show one gradient-descent step.

nodes.title: Supervised machine learning
nodes.summary: Learn a mapping from inputs to labelled targets. Begin with a simple baseline and choose a metric that fits the task. Fit preprocessing on training data only.
nodes.question: Why fit a scaler only on the training split?
nodes.answer: Using held-out distribution statistics during fitting leaks information. Reuse training-derived parameters to transform validation and test data.
nodes.project: Train a simple classifier or regressor, compare with a trivial baseline and report held-out performance.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Train a simple classifier or regressor, compare with a trivial baseline and report held-out performance.

nodes.title: Unsupervised machine learning
nodes.summary: Clustering groups examples under a chosen geometry; dimensionality reduction finds useful representations. A cluster is not automatically a true category or causal explanation.
nodes.question: Why can feature scaling change k-means clusters?
nodes.answer: Distance depends on numerical scale. A high-range feature can dominate Euclidean distances, so scaling choices change the geometry and the result.
nodes.project: Cluster a tiny two-dimensional dataset and compare assignments before and after scaling.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Cluster a tiny two-dimensional dataset and compare assignments before and after scaling.

nodes.title: Neural networks & deep learning
nodes.summary: Compose parameterized transformations and nonlinearities, define a loss, then backpropagate derivatives. Depth alone does not guarantee better generalization. Monitor validation loss and numerical stability.
nodes.question: What does backpropagation compute, and what does an optimizer do?
nodes.answer: Backpropagation computes loss gradients using the chain rule. An optimizer uses those gradients and its update rule to change parameters. These are separate operations.
nodes.project: Build a two-layer network on a toy task and test one parameter gradient.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Build a two-layer network on a toy task and test one parameter gradient.

nodes.title: PyTorch training workflow
nodes.summary: Tensors, autograd, data loaders and explicit train/evaluation modes form the training loop. Clear gradients appropriately and keep evaluation separate from parameter updates.
nodes.question: Why call zero_grad before another independent training step?
nodes.answer: Gradients accumulate by default. Clearing them prevents accidental addition across steps unless deliberate gradient accumulation is intended.
nodes.project: Train a tiny network, save a checkpoint and reproduce its evaluation predictions.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Train a tiny network, save a checkpoint and reproduce its evaluation predictions.

nodes.title: TensorFlow alternative
nodes.summary: TensorFlow and Keras provide another tensor and training ecosystem. This is an optional alternative exploration; learning both frameworks is not a prerequisite for RAG or transformers.
nodes.question: What should stay comparable when porting a model between frameworks?
nodes.answer: Data splits, preprocessing, architecture, loss, optimization settings and evaluation protocol should match. Numerical details can still produce small differences.
nodes.project: Recreate one small trained model in Keras and compare held-out predictions.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Recreate one small trained model in Keras and compare held-out predictions.

nodes.title: Text processing & documents
nodes.summary: Treat text as versioned data. Preserve document IDs, encoding, source information and boundaries. Normalization can help search but can also destroy meaningful distinctions such as code case.
nodes.question: Why retain source IDs after cleaning and chunking documents?
nodes.answer: IDs let you trace a passage to its source, update changed documents, inspect citations and avoid duplicate ingestion. Keep offsets or passage IDs too.
nodes.project: Load three UTF-8 notes into records containing stable IDs, titles and text.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Load three UTF-8 notes into records containing stable IDs, titles and text.

nodes.title: Tokenization
nodes.summary: Tokenizers map text into token IDs according to a vocabulary and encoding procedure. Tokens need not be whole words. The tokenizer and model vocabulary must agree.
nodes.question: Why is word count not the same as token count?
nodes.answer: A word can split into several subword or byte tokens; whitespace, symbols and language affect segmentation. Use the model tokenizer when measuring its context budget.
nodes.project: Compare character and word tokenizers on punctuation, Unicode and unseen words.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Compare character and word tokenizers on punctuation, Unicode and unseen words.

nodes.title: Embeddings & similarity
nodes.summary: An embedding maps an item to a vector. Similarity reflects the model and training objective, not guaranteed truth. Retrieval can use pretrained embeddings without training your own model.
nodes.question: Does a high cosine similarity prove two passages say the same thing?
nodes.answer: No. It measures direction similarity in a particular representation. Negation, numbers and fine distinctions can still be wrong; evaluate retrieved passages against labelled questions.
nodes.project: Rank a few toy vectors by cosine similarity; explain zero-vector handling.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Rank a few toy vectors by cosine similarity; explain zero-vector handling.

nodes.title: Word2Vec: optional historical branch
nodes.summary: Word2Vec learns word vectors from local context prediction. Static word vectors give one representation per vocabulary entry, unlike contextual representations that depend on the surrounding text.
nodes.question: How would static and contextual embeddings handle the two meanings of bank?
nodes.answer: A static word vector shares one representation for bank. A contextual model can produce different representations for river bank and financial bank.
nodes.project: Write two ambiguous sentences and compare what static versus contextual representations can express.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Write two ambiguous sentences and compare what static versus contextual representations can express.

nodes.title: Attention & self-attention
nodes.summary: Scaled dot-product attention computes softmax(Q Kᵀ / sqrt(d_k)) V. In self-attention, queries, keys and values are derived from the same input sequence. A causal mask blocks access to future tokens.
nodes.question: If Q and K are T by d_k, what is the shape of their attention score matrix?
nodes.answer: Q K-transpose has shape T by T. Each row compares one query position with key positions. Row-wise softmax creates weights before multiplication with V.
nodes.project: Compute a two-token attention example and verify that each softmax row sums to one.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Compute a two-token attention example and verify that each softmax row sums to one.

nodes.title: Multi-head attention
nodes.summary: Different learned projections create attention heads. Their outputs are concatenated and projected back into the model representation. Heads are not guaranteed to have human-interpretable roles.
nodes.question: For d_model=64 and 4 equal heads, what is each head dimension?
nodes.answer: The conventional equal-head setup uses 16 dimensions per head. Concatenating four head outputs restores 64 dimensions before the output projection.
nodes.project: Trace batch, head, sequence and feature dimensions through a four-head attention block.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Trace batch, head, sequence and feature dimensions through a four-head attention block.

nodes.title: Positional information
nodes.summary: Attention needs a way to represent order. Original transformers use positional encodings; other designs use learned positions or rotary transformations. Positional methods have different extrapolation behavior.
nodes.question: Why does a transformer need positional information?
nodes.answer: Without positional information or order-sensitive structure, self-attention alone does not encode sequence order. Position representations distinguish permutations of otherwise identical tokens.
nodes.project: Compare representations of the same tokens in two orders with and without position information.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Compare representations of the same tokens in two orders with and without position information.

nodes.title: Transformer architecture
nodes.summary: Combine attention, feed-forward layers, residual connections and normalization. Encoder, decoder and encoder-decoder designs serve different objectives. A GPT-style decoder uses causal attention.
nodes.question: What prevents next-token training from seeing the target token through future positions?
nodes.answer: Inputs and targets are shifted appropriately and causal attention masks future positions. Dataset construction and masking must both avoid target leakage.
nodes.project: Draw a decoder block with tensor shapes and test a causal mask on a tiny input.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Draw a decoder block with tensor shapes and test a causal mask on a tiny input.

nodes.title: Use a local LLM
nodes.summary: Inference uses learned weights and a supplied context to generate token predictions. Sampling affects variability; it does not verify facts. Keep a fixed test prompt set and record model and settings.
nodes.question: How do context, retrieval and training differ?
nodes.answer: Context is temporary input. Retrieval selects information to supply as context. Training changes learned parameters. A long prompt does not update model weights.
nodes.project: Compare two prompts on the same local model, recording settings, latency and one failure.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Compare two prompts on the same local model, recording settings, latency and one failure.

nodes.title: Safety, privacy & source boundaries
nodes.summary: Treat model outputs and retrieved documents as untrusted. Validate tool arguments in code, minimize permissions, and keep actions bounded. Prompt instructions alone cannot enforce a security boundary.
nodes.question: What should happen if a retrieved document asks the assistant to delete files?
nodes.answer: Treat it as document content, not an authorized instruction. The application should lack that tool or require independently validated authorization before any such action.
nodes.project: Add a hostile document to a retrieval fixture and verify that no tool action can execute.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Add a hostile document to a retrieval fixture and verify that no tool action can execute.

nodes.title: Evaluation & regression sets
nodes.summary: Separate retrieval metrics from answer quality. Keep answerable, unanswerable and adversarial examples, with expected sources. Reserve held-out examples to assess changes after development.
nodes.question: Can perfect retrieval recall guarantee a correct generated answer?
nodes.answer: No. The model can ignore or misread relevant evidence. Evaluate support, citation correctness, abstention and latency separately from retrieval recall.
nodes.project: Create ten answerable and five unanswerable questions; record expected sources and a baseline.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Create ten answerable and five unanswerable questions; record expected sources and a baseline.

nodes.title: RAG & keyword retrieval
nodes.summary: A RAG pipeline retrieves passages and supplies them as evidence for generation. BM25 provides a useful lexical baseline and does not require embedding training. Show evidence before trusting an answer.
nodes.question: When is RAG more appropriate than fine-tuning?
nodes.answer: RAG is useful when answers require changing or inspectable external facts. Fine-tuning adapts behavior or task performance; it is not a reliable substitute for a versioned document store.
nodes.project: Use Ask your sources to inspect four passages; record supported answers and abstentions.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Use Ask your sources to inspect four passages; record supported answers and abstentions.

nodes.title: Vector & hybrid retrieval
nodes.summary: Dense retrieval compares embeddings; lexical retrieval matches terms. Hybrid systems combine signals, often followed by reranking. Measure gains on the same questions before adding infrastructure.
nodes.question: Why retain lexical retrieval alongside embeddings?
nodes.answer: Exact identifiers and rare terms can be important. Embeddings can help paraphrases. Their strengths differ, so a measured hybrid system can improve coverage.
nodes.project: Compare lexical and embedding rankings for exact-ID and paraphrase questions; record recall at k.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Compare lexical and embedding rankings for exact-ID and paraphrase questions; record recall at k.

nodes.title: Tool-using agents
nodes.summary: An agent delegates some action selection to a model. Explicit tool contracts, state, step budgets, timeouts and traces make behavior inspectable. Begin with a predictable workflow and add decisions only where needed.
nodes.question: What stops an agent from repeatedly calling a failing tool?
nodes.answer: Enforced step/time budgets, retry limits and state checks outside the model. A prompt asking it to stop is not a sufficient operational control.
nodes.project: Implement a read-only search tool with argument validation, a two-step budget and a timeout test.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Implement a read-only search tool with argument validation, a two-step budget and a timeout test.

nodes.title: Multi-agent systems & MCP
nodes.summary: Multiple agents can divide tasks but add coordination and failure modes. MCP standardizes connections to tools and resources; it does not itself create a planner or validate every tool action.
nodes.question: When would two agents be worse than one deterministic workflow?
nodes.answer: When coordination, duplicated calls or conflicting state cost more than any task specialization helps. Compare success rate, latency and trace complexity against a simpler baseline.
nodes.project: Compare one workflow with a planner/reviewer pair on fixed tasks; retain only measured improvements.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Compare one workflow with a planner/reviewer pair on fixed tasks; retain only measured improvements.

nodes.title: Pretraining a tiny language model
nodes.summary: Pretraining learns an objective such as next-token prediction from a corpus. Split data carefully, estimate token and compute budgets and train a tiny example before scaling. A laptop exercise is not frontier-model training.
nodes.question: Why keep validation text separate before creating overlapping token windows?
nodes.answer: Overlapping windows can otherwise leak nearly identical text across splits, making validation loss too optimistic. Split at meaningful source boundaries before windowing.
nodes.project: Train or specify a tiny decoder experiment with data splits, loss curve and a saved checkpoint.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Train or specify a tiny decoder experiment with data splits, loss curve and a saved checkpoint.

nodes.title: Fine-tuning & LoRA
nodes.summary: Fine-tuning starts with pretrained weights and adapts them to a task. LoRA trains low-rank updates to selected matrices. Smaller trainable parameter counts do not eliminate activation memory or data-quality requirements.
nodes.question: Does LoRA mean the model needs no GPU or no base weights?
nodes.answer: No. Base weights still participate in computation, and activations use memory. Hardware feasibility depends on model, precision, context, batch size and implementation.
nodes.project: Design a small adapter comparison against the unchanged model using a held-out task set.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Design a small adapter comparison against the unchanged model using a held-out task set.

nodes.title: Reinforcement learning
nodes.summary: An agent learns behavior from rewards over interactions. Credit assignment and exploration differ from supervised target prediction. A reward function can reward unintended shortcuts.
nodes.question: Why is a high reward not automatically evidence of desirable behavior?
nodes.answer: The reward may omit important goals or be exploitable. Test actual task outcomes and side effects independently of the optimized score.
nodes.project: Simulate a small bandit and compare greedy and exploratory action selection.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Simulate a small bandit and compare greedy and exploratory action selection.

nodes.title: RLHF, preferences & alignment
nodes.summary: RLHF often uses preference data and a learned reward with policy optimization. Preference methods such as DPO offer a different training approach. Alignment is broader than one reward or tuning recipe.
nodes.question: Is DPO the same procedure as PPO with an explicit learned reward model?
nodes.answer: No. DPO optimizes a preference objective directly relative to a reference policy; PPO-based RLHF typically includes reward modeling and policy optimization. Neither guarantees safety.
nodes.project: Diagram SFT, reward-model/PPO and direct-preference workflows, including evaluation and data limits.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Diagram SFT, reward-model/PPO and direct-preference workflows, including evaluation and data limits.

nodes.title: Quantization & model memory
nodes.summary: Lower-precision weights can reduce storage and memory. Total runtime memory also includes activations, KV cache and runtime overhead. Compare quality and latency with fixed settings.
nodes.question: Why can a model fail to fit even when its weight file is smaller than available RAM?
nodes.answer: The loaded model needs additional memory for caches, buffers, activations and the runtime. Context and batch size can increase those requirements.
nodes.project: Estimate weight memory for a toy parameter count, then list runtime costs excluded from the estimate.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Estimate weight memory for a toy parameter count, then list runtime costs excluded from the estimate.

nodes.title: Inference & training optimization
nodes.summary: Profile before optimizing. KV caching avoids recomputing previous keys and values during autoregressive inference; attention kernels and batching change throughput and memory tradeoffs. Training has a different workload.
nodes.question: Why can a longer context increase memory even with quantized weights?
nodes.answer: Attention state and KV caches grow with sequence length and batch size. Weight compression does not automatically compress all runtime state.
nodes.project: Measure latency on a fixed workload at two context sizes and separate prefill from generation.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Measure latency on a fixed workload at two context sizes and separate prefill from generation.

nodes.title: Scaling laws & compute budgets
nodes.summary: Empirical scaling laws describe relationships among loss, model size, data and compute within studied settings. They guide budgets but are not universal guarantees for every architecture or task.
nodes.question: Why is an observed power-law trend not a guarantee for an arbitrary model?
nodes.answer: It is an empirical fit over particular experiments. Data quality, architecture, optimization and regime changes can invalidate extrapolation.
nodes.project: Plot a hypothetical loss-versus-compute curve and label measured points separately from extrapolations.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Plot a hypothetical loss-versus-compute curve and label measured points separately from extrapolations.

nodes.title: Distributed training
nodes.summary: Data, tensor and pipeline parallelism split different parts of the workload. Communication, synchronization and failures affect scaling. Study on diagrams or tiny processes before needing multiple GPUs.
nodes.question: How do data and tensor parallelism differ?
nodes.answer: Data parallel workers process different batches with replicated model parameters and synchronize gradients. Tensor parallelism partitions tensor computations or parameters across workers.
nodes.project: Draw two-worker data parallelism and identify where gradients synchronize and communication costs arise.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Draw two-worker data parallelism and identify where gradients synchronize and communication costs arise.

nodes.title: Laptop, Android & Pi delivery
nodes.summary: Run experiments on the laptop, use Android for cached reading and downloaded audio, and use a confirmed Pi model for lightweight serving. Device capability is measured, not inferred from a marketing name.
nodes.question: Why does opening localhost on Android not connect to the laptop?
nodes.answer: Localhost refers to the device running the browser. Use a deliberately configured network service or copy static files/audio; the local model bridge here is loopback-only.
nodes.project: Copy one WAV and transcript to Android; test playback with screen locked and record device details.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Copy one WAV and transcript to Android; test playback with screen locked and record device details.

checks: Load UTF-8 text with stable IDs
Reject duplicate IDs and handle empty files
Save a test command and expected output

projects.brief: Use the local source-search lab first, then add a downloaded model when hardware permits. Carry your fixtures and source IDs forward.
checks: Ten answerable and five unanswerable questions
Record model/version or retrieval-only mode, latency and failures

projects.brief: Train a deliberately small decoder or produce a reproducible experiment specification until hardware is available.
